issues.legal_issue: A tenant’s possession does not become adverse while the tenancy continues through statutory eviction proceedings or during a permitted period to vacate.
material_facts: The tenant’s status as a tenant was confirmed in eviction proceedings and remained so until the statutory revision was dismissed.
The revisional court then allowed the tenant three months to vacate, during which the tenant occupied the property permissively.
The owner filed a title-based possession suit within twelve years after that permitted period ended.
issues.conclusion: Adverse possession could not begin before the permitted period to vacate expired, and the possession suit was filed in time.
issues.legal_principle: The landlord-tenant relationship continues during the eviction proceedings, including an appeal and statutory revision, until the eviction order is finally confirmed. Where the court permits the tenant to remain for a further period to vacate, possession during that period is permissive, not adverse. The Court applied the twelve-year period relevant to the claim based on title; it relied on no earlier case in deciding this issue.

predicates.possession_suit: An owner brought a suit to recover possession of property from an occupant.
predicates.tenancy_continued_through_statutory_revi: The occupant's tenancy continued while the eviction dispute proceeded through statutory review.
predicates.tenant_permitted_to_remain_after_review: After the review ended, the court permitted the occupant to remain in the property for a period to vacate.
predicates.suit_filed_within_limitation_after_permi: The owner filed the possession suit within the applicable limitation period measured from the end of the permitted occupation.

issues.definition: When an occupant remains a tenant through statutory review, is then permitted to remain for a period to vacate, and the owner sues within the applicable limitation period after that permission ends, the possession suit is timely.

issues.legal_issue: A separate possession suit based on a fresh cause of action and title is not barred as a proceeding to execute an earlier eviction order.
material_facts: An earlier rent-control eviction proceeding resulted in an order against the occupant.
After a later notice, the owner brought a fresh eviction proceeding, in which the occupant asserted ownership by adverse possession.
The owner then filed the present suit for possession, relying on title and referring to the occupant’s assertion in the later proceeding, rather than seeking execution of the earlier eviction order.
issues.conclusion: The suit was not in reality a proceeding to execute the earlier eviction order, so the bar on separate suits for matters relating to execution did not apply.
issues.legal_principle: Section 47(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, as it stood before the 1976 amendment, requires questions between parties relating to execution, discharge, or satisfaction of a decree to be determined by the executing court rather than by a separate suit. The Court held that this restriction did not apply because the suit was based on title and a fresh cause of action, not on enforcement of the earlier eviction order.

rule.if: separate_possession_suit and earlier_eviction_order_exists and suit_based_on_title_and_fresh_cause and suit_does_not_seek_execution_of_earlier_order

predicates.separate_possession_suit: An owner brought a separate suit to recover possession from an occupant.
predicates.earlier_eviction_order_exists: An earlier proceeding resulted in an eviction order concerning the same occupant and property.
predicates.suit_based_on_title_and_fresh_cause: The owner based the later suit on title and on a fresh assertion or denial of rights by the occupant.
predicates.suit_does_not_seek_execution_of_earlier_: The owner sought possession through the later suit rather than asking the court to enforce the earlier eviction order.

issues.definition: A separate possession suit based on title and a fresh cause of action, rather than enforcement of an earlier eviction order, is not barred as an execution proceeding.

issues.legal_issue: An owner may bring a timely title-based possession suit after execution of an earlier tenancy-based eviction decree becomes time-barred, unless the owner’s title has been extinguished.
material_facts: The earlier eviction proceeding was based on the landlord-tenant relationship, and execution of its eviction order was not pursued within the applicable time.
The later suit was based on the owner’s title, not on the earlier decree.
The occupant had not acquired title by adverse possession when the later suit was filed, and the owner’s title had not otherwise been extinguished.
issues.conclusion: The later title-based possession suit was maintainable and was not barred by Sections 11 or 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure merely because execution of the earlier eviction order was time-barred.
issues.legal_principle: A title-based suit is distinct from an earlier suit based on tenancy, and the failure to execute the earlier decree does not by itself extinguish title or bar a later suit. The Court relied on Kutti Ali v. Chindan, Amina v. Ahmad, Raghunath Singh v. Hansraj Kunwar, Viroopakshan v. Chambu Nayar, Mhadaagonda Ramgonda Patil v. Shripal Balwant Rainade, Maganlal v. Jaiswal Industries, and Harbans Singh v. Guran Ditta Singh. It applied Sections 11 and 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure and distinguished cases where the underlying right itself had been extinguished or the later suit merely sought to rely on an earlier time-barred decree.

rule.if: title_based_possession_suit and earlier_eviction_decree_based_on_tenancy and execution_of_earlier_decree_time_barred and owner_title_not_extinguished and suit_filed_within_limitation

predicates.title_based_possession_suit: An owner brought a suit to recover possession on the basis of ownership rather than on the basis of a tenancy.
predicates.earlier_eviction_decree_based_on_tenancy: An earlier eviction decree was based on the landlord-tenant relationship between the parties.
predicates.execution_of_earlier_decree_time_barred: The time allowed to enforce the earlier decree expired before it was executed.
predicates.owner_title_not_extinguished: The occupant had not acquired ownership by adverse possession and the owner's title had not otherwise ended.
predicates.suit_filed_within_limitation: The owner brought the later suit within the applicable limitation period.

issues.definition: A timely title-based possession suit is maintainable after execution of a tenancy-based eviction decree becomes time-barred if the owner’s title remains unextinguished.
